overview: The later kingdom of Scotland joined regions with different languages, traditions and political histories. Its surviving record includes trading towns, universities, churches and royal documents. The atlas interval 1000-1715 is map coverage: political union with England occurred in 1707, and Scotland's communities continued afterward.

periods.title: Kingdom and burghs
periods.summary: Royal centres, ports and market towns supported trade, while war and diplomacy shaped relations with neighbouring rulers.

periods.title: Learning and religious change
periods.summary: The university at St Andrews began in 1413; the Reformation transformed church life in 1560.

periods.title: Within Great Britain
periods.summary: The kingdoms united in 1707, before the imported Scotland segment ends.

sections.title: What a town ate and threw away

items.text: Waterlogged deposits in medieval Perth preserved plant remains from floors, rubbish pits and latrines. Many come from the 1100s-1200s. Things discarded in a damp backyard can be better evidence for dinner than a royal chronicle.

Perth's plant remains include oats and barley, with less wheat, alongside berries, apples and hazelnuts. Figs, grapes and walnuts point to imported foods. Their presence shows access, not that every household enjoyed the same menu.

Moss was gathered for several purposes, including bedding and toilet hygiene. Archaeologists must use context to distinguish those activities. Medieval shopping lists could include useful plants that a modern supermarket would put nowhere near the food aisle.

Perth's narrow property plots accommodated households and urban trades, including work on animal skins. The town's river crossing and overseas connections linked local labour to distant customers. This urban evidence cannot stand for all Scottish homes.

The Lewis hoard contains 93 gaming objects, including pieces from at least four chess sets. Most were carved from walrus ivory, probably in Norway around 1200; some used whale teeth. Their thrones, clothing and faces preserve a carver's close attention to detail.

Lewis belonged to the Norwegian kingdom when the chess pieces were probably buried. The Isles passed to Scotland in 1266. Including them here shows the changing regional history, not that a Scottish royal workshop necessarily made them.

No one securely knows who buried the pieces or why. A merchant's stock and a local powerful owner's possessions are possibilities. The discovery accounts also conflict. Treasure can produce excellent questions without supplying a complete adventure story.

Teaching began at St Andrews in 1410, and papal documents formally established its university in 1413. Organized higher learning was an achievement, but admission to such study was far narrower than access to a modern school.

St Andrews Castle preserves a mine and countermine associated with its 1546-47 siege. Attackers dug toward the defenses while defenders dug to intercept them. The surviving tunnels make military engineering visible beneath a former bishop's residence.

The Protestant Reformation of 1560 changed church institutions and worship. St Andrews Castle's history includes religious conflict before that turning point. Religious change was lived through buildings, communities and authority, not simply one ruler choosing a new label.

The 1320 Declaration of Arbroath appealed to the pope on behalf of the kingdom's political community. It argued for independence under Robert Bruce. A forceful diplomatic letter states its authors' case; it is not a survey of every inhabitant's opinions.

The letter's Latin includes propter libertatem solummodo, “for freedom alone.” This follows the National Records of Scotland's scholarly text of the 1320 letter. The archive distinguishes that edition from an exact transcription of its surviving document; Latin was an international language of diplomacy.

ending.text: On 1 May 1707 Scotland and England became the kingdom of Great Britain with a shared parliament. Scotland retained important legal institutions, and its people, languages and regional identities continued. The atlas's 1715 boundary is not the date of this union and should not be presented as Scotland's disappearance.
